She denied any history of skin rash or mucosal ulcerations. No history of fever. Clinical examination reveals limited lumbar spine movements and active arthritis at both knees bilaterally. She also has tenderness over the Achilles tendon (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: lower back pain associated with morning stiffness
why_right: Low back pain for 3 months with morning stiffness of about 1 hour is inflammatory back pain. Add limited lumbar spine movement, a lower limb large joint peripheral arthritis (knees, ankles) and Achilles tenderness (enthesitis) and the picture is axial spondyloarthritis, i.e. ankylosing spondylitis. The absence of rash, mucosal ulcers and fever removes the main mimics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reactive arthritis needs a preceding GI or GU infection and often conjunctivitis or urethritis; none is described here, and it is usually an acute oligoarthritis rather than chronic axial disease.
B. Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric small joint polyarthritis (MCP, PIP, wrists) that spares the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints and does not typically cause Achilles enthesitis.
D. Crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout) gives acute, episodic, very painful mono or oligoarthritis, not 3 months of inflammatory back pain with restricted lumbar movement.
key_concept:
Inflammatory back pain >3 months + enthesitis + limited lumbar motion = ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Inflammatory back pain: morning stiffness, better with activity, worse with rest, night pain
  • Peripheral: lower limb large joint arthritis (classically asymmetric oligoarthritis), Achilles enthesitis (heel pain)
  • Extra-articular: anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, apical lung fibrosis
  • Diagnosis: sacroiliitis on imaging (MRI most sensitive early), HLA-B27
  • Treatment: NSAIDs first, then TNF inhibitors
exam_pearl: A woman does not exclude AS: chronic inflammatory back pain plus enthesitis is the key, not the sex.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1605).
Compiler note: Screenshot labelled 0190; C highlighted and Answer: C.

stem: A 40-year-old man with paraplegia following road traffic accident one year ago is brought to the Emergency Department because of sudden onset dyspnea and chest pain. On examination, he is in severe distress and cyanosed. He has left parasternal heave and loud P2. Chest is clear to auscultation (see lab results and reports). Blood pressure 80/55 mmHg Heart rate 110/min Respiratory rate 30/min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 86 % Test Result Normal Values ABG HCO3- 22 22-28 mmol/L ABG PCO2 4.2 4.7-6.0 kPa pH 7.4 7.36-7.45 ABG PO2 8.6 10.6-14.2 kPa Echocardiogram: Dilated right ventricle with pulmonary artery pressure of 55 mmHg. Venous Doppler: Confirmed DVT in the left leg extending to the thigh. Which of the following is the best line of management?
why_right: Paraplegia means long-term immobilization, and the confirmed proximal DVT plus sudden dyspnea, chest pain, cyanosis and SpO2 86% make this acute pulmonary embolism. The decisive clue is BP 80/55 with HR 110: this is high-risk (massive) PE with shock, and right heart strain is confirmed by the parasternal heave, loud P2 and a dilated RV on echo. Unstable PE is treated with systemic thrombolysis, so an alteplase infusion is the best line of management.
why_wrong_block:
A. An IVC filter only stops new emboli and does nothing for the clot already obstructing the pulmonary circulation; it is used when anticoagulation is contraindicated or PE recurs despite adequate anticoagulation.
C. LMWH is the treatment for hemodynamically stable PE; with hypotension it is too slow to relieve the obstruction, so thrombolysis comes first (heparin follows).
D. Warfarin takes days to work and is long-term secondary prevention, never the acute treatment of PE with shock.
key_concept:
Acute PE: the blood pressure decides the treatment.
  • Hypotension or shock (massive PE): thrombolysis (alteplase)
  • Thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: surgical or catheter embolectomy
  • Stable PE: anticoagulation (LMWH or DOAC)
  • IVC filter: anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrence despite it
  • RV strain signs: parasternal heave, loud P2, dilated RV on echo
exam_pearl: The same PE with a normal blood pressure flips the answer to enoxaparin; hypotension is what makes it alteplase.

stem: A 62-year-old patient with a known case of chronic hepatitis C presented with abdominal pain and swelling. Examination showed ascites, abdominal tenderness and peripheral edema. Diagnostic ascitic tap done and revealed a neutrophil count of 400/mm (<250 mm) Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 90 /min Temperature 37.6 °C Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the management?
why_right: A cirrhotic patient (chronic hepatitis C) with ascites who develops abdominal pain and tenderness has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proven otherwise. The diagnostic tap confirms it: ascitic neutrophils 400/mm3, above the 250 threshold, even though the fever is only low grade (37.6). SBP is treated with IV antibiotics, classically a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, started without waiting for culture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluid restriction is part of routine ascites care (mainly for dilutional hyponatremia) and does not treat an infected peritoneum.
B. Spironolactone is the first-line diuretic for uncomplicated cirrhotic ascites; it would be the answer if the neutrophil count were below 250 with no infection.
D. Large-volume paracentesis is for tense or diuretic-refractory ascites; it does not treat SBP, which must be covered with antibiotics first.
key_concept:
Ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm3 = SBP = IV antibiotics.
  • Ascites with abdominal pain in cirrhosis: tap and treat as SBP
  • SBP first line: IV third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone)
  • Uncomplicated ascites: sodium restriction, then spironolactone, add furosemide
  • Tense or refractory ascites: therapeutic paracentesis
exam_pearl: SBP often has little or no fever; the neutrophil count, not the temperature, makes the diagnosis.

stem: Women had a wound from the garden and the nurse found that the pt had tetanus vaccine 12 years ago. What to do ?
why_right: A garden wound is soil-contaminated, so it counts as a tetanus-prone (dirty) wound. For a dirty wound a booster is due if the last tetanus dose was more than 5 years ago, and hers was 12 years ago, so she needs a booster now. An adult booster is given as Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis), which also refreshes pertussis protection; tetanus immunoglobulin is not needed when the primary series was completed.
why_wrong_block: A. "Tetanus shot" is vague: it does not specify the booster form, and a tetanus-only shot misses the diphtheria and pertussis protection that Tdap gives; it is also not tetanus immunoglobulin, which is only for unknown or incomplete vaccination with a dirty wound.
key_concept:
Tetanus wound prophylaxis depends on the wound type and the time since the last dose.
  • Clean minor wound: booster if last dose >10 years ago
  • Dirty or tetanus-prone wound: booster if last dose >5 years ago
  • Unknown or fewer than 3 doses: vaccine, plus TIG if the wound is dirty
  • Adult booster of choice: Tdap if not given before, otherwise Td or Tdap
exam_pearl: Do not apply the 10-year rule to a dirty wound; soil contamination drops the cutoff to 5 years.

stem: 28-year-old woman with active neuropsychiatric lupus based on clinical manifestations and her workups. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy?
why_right: Active neuropsychiatric lupus is organ- and life-threatening SLE, so it needs induction with high-dose corticosteroids plus an immunosuppressant. Cyclophosphamide is the preferred immunosuppressant for severe inflammatory neuropsychiatric lupus. The lead-in asks for first-line therapy, so the combination of corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide is the answer.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cyclophosphamide alone omits the high-dose corticosteroid that is part of first-line induction; the two are given together.
C. Rituximab is reserved for refractory disease that fails steroids and cyclophosphamide, not first line.
D. Steroids alone are not enough for life-threatening lupus; they would suit mild flares, while severe organ involvement needs an added immunosuppressant.
key_concept:
SLE treatment scales with organ threat.
  • All patients: hydroxychloroquine as the cornerstone
  • Mild (skin, joints): hydroxychloroquine with NSAID or low-dose steroid
  • Severe (neuropsychiatric, renal): high-dose steroid plus cyclophosphamide
  • Refractory: rituximab
exam_pearl: Pick the combination: in severe lupus, steroid alone and cyclophosphamide alone are both traps.

stem: 55-year-old obese non-smoker man with hypertension presents with exertional dyspnea for 2 years. His wife stated that he is uncomfortable while sleeping at night and produces loud snores. Examination revealed central cyanosis, suffused conjunctivae and clear chest. BMI 40 kg/m2 Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
why_right: An obese (BMI 40) man with loud snoring and disturbed sleep reported by his wife has obstructive sleep apnea until proven otherwise. Hypertension is a recognised complication, and central cyanosis with suffused conjunctivae (hypoxemia with secondary polycythemia) and a clear chest point to a sleep-related breathing problem, not a lung disease. Polysomnography (overnight sleep study) is the diagnostic test, so it has the highest diagnostic value here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spirometry diagnoses obstructive lung disease such as asthma or COPD; this non-smoker has a clear chest and a sleep history, not airway disease.
B. Spiral CT (CT pulmonary angiography) is for suspected pulmonary embolism with sudden dyspnea; this is a 2-year picture with snoring.
D. Methacholine challenge confirms asthma when spirometry is normal but symptoms suggest it; there is no wheeze or trigger history here.
key_concept:
Snoring + obesity + daytime or night symptoms = OSA → polysomnography.
  • Clues: loud snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, obesity, hypertension
  • Diagnosis: polysomnography
  • Treatment: weight loss plus nasal CPAP
  • Cyanosis, plethora and hypercapnia suggest obesity hypoventilation overlap
exam_pearl: "Highest diagnostic value" for a snorer is the sleep study, not a lung test, even when dyspnea is the complaint.

stem: A 43-year-old man who is known to have chronic hepatitis B presents to the clinic for evaluation. He is asymptomatic with normal physical examination (see lab results and report). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option? Test Result Normal Values RBC 5 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) 4.2-5.4 x 1012/L (Female) Hb 11.9 130-170 g/L. (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 145 150-400 x 109/L WBC 3.9 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Direct bilirubin 17 1.5-6.5 mol/L Total bilirubin 21 3.5-16.5 mol/L Aspartate aminotransferase 89 12-40 IU/L Alanine aminotransferase 61 5-40 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 160 39-117 IU/L US Abdomen: Showed mild coarse liver echotexture.
why_right: This chronic hepatitis B patient has raised transaminases (AST 89, ALT 61), a coarse liver on ultrasound, and low platelets and WBC that suggest evolving fibrosis with portal hypertension. Active liver injury and possible cirrhosis are indications to start antiviral therapy even though he is asymptomatic. Entecavir is a first-line oral agent because it is potent and has a high barrier to resistance.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation fits inactive carriers with normal liver enzymes and low viral load; this patient has raised enzymes and signs of liver damage.
C. Lamivudine has a low barrier to resistance with high resistance rates, so it is no longer first line.
D. Pegylated interferon has many side effects and is avoided with cytopenias and possible advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, as here.
key_concept:
Chronic HBV: treat when the liver is being damaged.
  • Raised ALT/AST or significant fibrosis or cirrhosis: start antiviral
  • First line: entecavir or tenofovir (potent, high resistance barrier)
  • Normal LFTs with low viral load: observe and monitor
  • Lamivudine: outdated because of resistance
exam_pearl: Low platelets and a coarse liver in HBV mean cirrhosis is developing: treat, do not watch.

stem: 70-year-old man heavy smoker, presents with left sided chest pain and hemoptysis. On examination, he has lost the angle of finger nail ( I don't remember the rest ) Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 85 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 92 % Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: lost the angle of finger nail
why_right: A 70-year-old heavy smoker with chest pain and hemoptysis is lung cancer until proven otherwise. The loss of the nail angle is finger clubbing, which in a smoker strongly suggests bronchogenic carcinoma. Low-grade hypoxemia (SpO2 92%) with normal vitals otherwise fits a chronic process rather than an acute event.
why_wrong_block:
A. COPD fits a heavy smoker, but it does not cause clubbing; clubbing in a COPD patient should prompt a search for lung cancer.
B. Bronchiectasis does cause hemoptysis and clubbing, but it presents with chronic copious purulent sputum, usually in a younger patient; it would be chosen with that sputum history.
C. PE causes sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain and hemoptysis with tachycardia and a risk factor such as immobility; it does not cause clubbing, which takes weeks to develop.
key_concept:
Smoker + hemoptysis + clubbing = bronchogenic carcinoma.
  • Clubbing causes: lung cancer, bronchiectasis, lung abscess or empyema, interstitial fibrosis, cyanotic heart disease
  • COPD alone does not cause clubbing
  • Hoarseness: recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion
  • Painful wrists with clubbing: hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
exam_pearl: "Clubbing in COPD" is a trap: COPD does not club, so think cancer.

stem: A 35-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis for 6 months on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and ibuprofen daily presented to the clinic with increasing joint pain in both hands and feet associated with morning stiffness for 2-hours. On examination, he shows signs of active arthritis at both wrists. Hand X-rays show erosions at multiple joints (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment? Test Result Normal Values Hb 120 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Platelets count 450 150-400 × 109/L WBC 8 4.5-10.5 × 109/L ESR 60 2-10 mm/h (Male) 3-15 mm/h (Female) C-reactive peptide 18 <8.2 mg/L Rheumatoid factor 500 <58 klU/L
why_right: After 6 months on an adequate methotrexate dose (20 mg weekly), this patient still has active arthritis, 2-hour morning stiffness, high ESR and CRP, a very high RF, and erosions at multiple joints. Erosions and high-titre RF are poor prognostic factors, and failure of methotrexate in that setting is the indication to add a biologic. A TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab, added to methotrexate, is the most appropriate additional treatment.
why_wrong_block:
B. Azathioprine is not a standard RA DMARD to add after methotrexate failure; it is used mainly in lupus, vasculitis and transplant immunosuppression.
C. Cyclophosphamide is for severe organ-threatening disease such as lupus nephritis or rheumatoid vasculitis, not for erosive joint disease.
D. Hydroxychloroquine is a mild DMARD used in early or mild RA or in combination therapy; it is too weak once erosive disease has broken through methotrexate.
key_concept:
RA ladder: methotrexate first, then escalate when disease stays active.
  • First line DMARD: methotrexate
  • Active disease on methotrexate with poor prognostic factors (erosions, high RF or anti-CCP): add a biologic such as a TNF inhibitor
  • Without poor prognostic factors: combination conventional DMARDs is an option
  • Monitor activity with ESR and CRP
exam_pearl: Erosions on methotrexate are the signal for a biologic, not another weak DMARD.

stem: Patient underwent bone marrow transplantation due to SCD, developed febrile neutropenia , she was given Ceftazidime and shows no improvement After 72 Hours, what to add? (No Pneumonia , No Hypotension , No Central Line , No Skin/Mucus Ulcerations)
why_right: This post-bone-marrow-transplant patient is high risk, and fever has persisted despite an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (ceftazidime). The stem deliberately rules out every trigger for adding vancomycin: no pneumonia, no hypotension, no central line, no skin or mucosal lesions. Persistent fever in a profoundly neutropenic patient with no bacterial source points to an occult fungal infection, so the addition is an empirical antifungal, amphotericin B.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vancomycin is added only for specific indications such as hemodynamic instability, pneumonia, catheter-related or skin and soft-tissue infection, or MRSA; the stem excludes all of them.
B. Piperacillin-tazobactam is another antipseudomonal beta-lactam with essentially the same bacterial coverage as ceftazidime; it would be a swap, not an addition, and does nothing for a possible fungal infection.
C. Ceftriaxone has no antipseudomonal activity and is narrower than ceftazidime, so it adds nothing in febrile neutropenia.
key_concept:
Febrile neutropenia: start broad, then add only for a reason.
  • Initial: antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, meropenem, pip-tazo, ceftazidime)
  • Add vancomycin: shock, pneumonia, line or skin infection, MRSA
  • Persistent fever after 4 to 7 days of broad antibiotics, no source, high risk: add empirical antifungal
  • Antifungal options: amphotericin B, echinocandin (caspofungin), voriconazole
exam_pearl: When the stem lists "no line, no skin lesion, no pneumonia, no shock", it is telling you vancomycin is not the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: post chemo therapy, 7 days of fever and neutropenia, choice of treatment? IV ampho (anti-fungal) / Vancomycin / Azithromycin / Ciprofloxacin. Answer: A (IV amphotericin), consistent.

stem: 50 yo smoker one pack a day for 20 Years , he was hypertensive, physical exam unremarkable. Labs are normal except : LDL 8.7 BMI 21 For this patient What can help reduce the risk for cardiovascular disease?
OptA: Reduce smoking consumption gradually to promote cardiac health
OptB: Start low intensity cholesterol lowering agent
highlight_terms_source: smoker one pack a day for 20 Years
why_right: This 50-year-old has two major modifiable risks: 20 pack-years of active smoking and very high LDL. The listed statin option is low intensity, which is inadequate for an LDL this high (it needs high-intensity therapy), so it is not a correct choice. Stopping smoking gives a large cardiovascular risk reduction, and bupropion is an effective pharmacological aid to cessation, making it the option that truly lowers his risk.
why_wrong_block:
A. Gradual cutting down does not deliver the benefit of complete cessation; the goal is to quit, ideally with pharmacotherapy and counselling.
B. A statin is indicated, but low intensity is the wrong dose: LDL 8.7 mmol/L (about 335 mg/dL) is far above the 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL) cutoff that calls for a high-intensity statin, which is not offered.
D. Waiting for symptoms abandons primary prevention; risk factors should be treated before the first cardiac event.
key_concept:
Primary prevention: treat every modifiable risk factor now.
  • Smoking cessation aids: varenicline, NRT and bupropion are all first-line options
  • LDL ≥4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL): high-intensity statin regardless of risk score
  • Cutting down gradually is not the goal; complete cessation is
  • Also control blood pressure
exam_pearl: Read the statin intensity: "low intensity" for a very high LDL is the trap that makes it wrong.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Note: No High Intensity Statins (among the options).

stem: 40 years old male, Came to ER with one day history of left leg area swelling and pain. He mentioned history of insect bite. On examination there is erythema, pain and tenderness with irregular borders He was febrile 38.4 What is the initial step in management?
highlight_terms_source: erythema, pain and tenderness with irregular borders
why_right: An acute ("one day") painful, tender, erythematous leg after an "insect bite" (portal of entry) with "irregular borders" and fever of 38.4 is cellulitis. It is a clinical diagnosis, and the initial step is to start empirical antibiotics covering streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus; fever alone does not mandate tests before treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Doppler US: used when a swollen leg suggests DVT (calf swelling, risk factors, no skin portal of entry). Here the erythema, bite and fever point to infection; Doppler is only added if DVT remains a real concern.
B. Warm compresses and observe: acceptable only for a simple local bite reaction without fever. A febrile spreading erythema is an infection that needs antibiotics, and delay risks progression or sepsis.
C. CBC: may be sent but does not change the decision and is not required for uncomplicated cellulitis. It is useful when the patient is septic or immunocompromised, never in place of starting treatment.
key_concept:
Cellulitis = clinical diagnosis; treat empirically, do not wait for tests.
  • Cellulitis: poorly demarcated (irregular) erythema, deeper dermis/subcutis, strep or staph.
  • Erysipelas: sharply demarcated, raised, superficial, mostly group A strep, penicillin.
  • Mild, afebrile and well: oral antibiotics.
  • Systemic features, diabetes or failure of oral therapy: IV antibiotics.
  • Fluctuant collection: incise and drain (abscess).
  • Suspected DVT instead: Doppler US.
exam_pearl: Red, hot, tender leg with a portal of entry and fever = antibiotics first; Doppler only if the picture is swelling without skin infection.

stem: 50 something year old complaining of recurring chest pain mainly at night came to ER with acute episode of chest pain ecg showed st elevation in inferior leads that subside with sublingual nitrate coronary angiogram: no sclerotic changes what is the most app treatment long term
highlight_terms_source: recurring chest pain mainly at night
st elevation in inferior leads that subside with sublingual nitrate
why_right: Recurrent chest pain "mainly at night", transient inferior ST elevation that "subside[s] with sublingual nitrate", and a coronary angiogram with "no sclerotic changes" is vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina. Long-term therapy is a long-acting calcium channel blocker, which prevents coronary spasm; nitrates can be added for breakthrough attacks.
why_wrong_block:
B. Aspirin and BB: right for atherosclerotic angina or post MI. In vasospasm, beta blockers can worsen spasm (unopposed alpha vasoconstriction) and aspirin adds nothing with normal coronaries.
C. Aspirin and high dose statin: secondary prevention for atherosclerotic disease (ACS, plaque on angiography). The angiogram here is clean, so this does not treat the spasm causing his attacks.
key_concept:
Vasospastic angina: rest/night pain, transient ST elevation, normal coronaries, CCB.
  • Trigger features: night or early morning, at rest, smoking, cocaine, triptans.
  • ECG: transient ST elevation that resolves with nitrate.
  • Angiography: normal or non obstructive coronaries; provocation test (ergonovine/acetylcholine) confirms.
  • Treatment: long-acting CCB (nifedipine, diltiazem, amlodipine) plus nitrate as needed.
  • Avoid: non selective beta blockers.
exam_pearl: ST elevation that vanishes with nitrate and a clean angiogram = spasm: give a CCB, not a beta blocker.

stem: Patient presented with tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a blood pressure of 220/100. Investigation confirmed the diagnosis of aortic dissection. Which of the following is the best next treatment?
highlight_terms_source: tearing chest pain radiating to the back
why_right: In confirmed aortic dissection with BP "220/100", the first treatment is an IV beta blocker such as esmolol to lower heart rate and the force of LV ejection (dP/dt), which limits propagation of the tear. Rate control must come before any vasodilator, and esmolol is short acting and titratable.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV Nitroprusside: used to further lower BP, but only after beta blockade. Given alone it causes reflex tachycardia and increases shear stress on the aortic wall.
C. Urgent surgical referral: needed for type A (ascending) dissection and complicated type B, but it runs in parallel with, not before, immediate IV rate and BP control.
D. Oral Amlodipine: too slow and not titratable for an emergency; oral agents are for long-term BP control after the acute phase.
key_concept:
Aortic dissection: beta blocker FIRST, then vasodilator, then decide surgery by type.
  • Clinical: tearing pain to the back, BP difference between arms, pulse deficit.
  • Stable: CT angiography; unstable: echocardiography (TEE).
  • Step 1: IV beta blocker (esmolol, labetalol) for HR and BP.
  • Step 2: add vasodilator (nitroprusside) if BP still high.
  • Type A (ascending): emergency surgery.
  • Uncomplicated type B (descending): medical therapy.
exam_pearl: Vasodilator before beta blocker = reflex tachycardia that extends the tear.

stem: A 69-year-old man is evaluated during a routine examination. He reports his blood pressure to be around 150/84 mmHg on several occasions. He is known to have mild benign prostatic hyperplasia, and hyperlipidemia for which he is taking simvastatin. Cardiac examination is normal, and the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show a normal chemistry panel; a urine dipstick demonstrates no blood or protein. An electrocardiogram shows no evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy Blood pressure 147/86 mmHg Heart rate 80 /min Respiratory rate 14 /min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 95 % BMI 31 kg/m2 Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Repeat blood pressure determination in 4 months
highlight_terms_source: blood pressure to be around 150/84 mmHg
no evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy
why_right: Repeated readings around "150/84" and "147/86" in a 69 year old are mild (stage 1) hypertension with no target organ damage: normal chemistry, no proteinuria, "no evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy". He is obese ("BMI 31") and has no diabetes, CKD or known cardiovascular disease, so the first step is lifestyle modification with weight loss, and drugs are added only if BP does not respond.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeat BP in 4 months: elevated BP is already documented on several occasions; waiting without any intervention wastes the chance to treat with lifestyle change now.
C. Start Amlodipine: a good first line drug for patients over 55, but in mild hypertension without organ damage it is started only if lifestyle change fails.
D. Start B-blockers: not first line for hypertension unless there is a compelling indication (ischemic heart disease, heart failure, rate control), and drug therapy is not yet indicated here.
key_concept:
Stage 1 HTN without organ damage: lifestyle first, drugs if no response.
  • Check organ damage: creatinine/electrolytes, urine protein/blood, ECG for LVH, fundi.
  • Lifestyle: weight loss, salt restriction, exercise, limit alcohol.
  • Drug now if: organ damage, diabetes, CKD, established CVD, high CVD risk, or stage 2 BP.
  • First drug: ACEI/ARB (under 55 or diabetic), CCB (over 55).
  • Beta blockers: only with a compelling indication.
exam_pearl: Obese patient with mild BP and clean workup: weight loss and lifestyle first; any organ damage or diabetes flips it to a drug.

stem: 68 woman with HTN (no medication) DM, Dyslipidemia came after transiet slurred speech for 30 minutes and resolved. no weakness no dyarthria or ataxia (written exactly like this) Her vitals: 160/80 the rest are normal (RR,HR, O2) What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: transiet slurred speech for 30 minutes and resolved
why_right: "Transient slurred speech for 30 minutes" that "resolved" is a TIA, and she has untreated hypertension ("no medication", BP "160/80") with diabetes and dyslipidemia. Secondary prevention requires BP control, and in a diabetic the first line antihypertensive is an ACE inhibitor (renoprotective); ACEI based therapy is also the classic choice after stroke/TIA.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lasix: a loop diuretic is for fluid overload (heart failure, edema, renal failure), not first line hypertension; the diuretic used in hypertension is a thiazide-like agent.
B. Amlodipine: first line for patients over 55 without diabetes, or as an add-on; in a diabetic patient an ACEI/ARB comes first.
C. Metoprolol: beta blockers are not first line for hypertension or stroke prevention; reserve for compelling indications such as ischemic heart disease, heart failure or rate control.
key_concept:
After TIA: antiplatelet + statin + BP control; diabetic hypertensive = ACEI/ARB.
  • Step 1, diabetic or under 55: ACEI or ARB.
  • Step 1, over 55 non diabetic: CCB.
  • Step 2: ACEI/ARB + CCB or thiazide-like diuretic.
  • TIA workup: brain imaging, carotid duplex, ECG for AF.
  • Also control diabetes and lipids (statin).
exam_pearl: Diabetes in the stem turns the first antihypertensive into an ACEI/ARB regardless of age.

stem: 30 something female Medically free complained of fever, arthralgia, oral ulcer and skin rash for 1 week. P/E skin eruption over the face and trunk. Immunology? Testing is ordered (No details about the type of rash or if the ulcer is painful, the q is mainly written like this) Many labs but the ones I remember are erythrocytes 30 and protein positive, ESR is high, no mention of ANA or anti Ds DNA What is the diagnosis ?
highlight_terms_source: fever, arthralgia, oral ulcer and skin rash
why_right: A young woman with "fever, arthralgia, oral ulcer and skin rash" over the "face", plus urine showing red cells and "protein positive" (renal involvement) and high ESR, fits multisystem SLE. Oral ulcers, arthritis, malar type rash and renal disease are all classic SLE criteria; ANA and anti dsDNA would confirm it.
why_wrong_block:
A. IgA vasculitis: mostly children, with palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks, abdominal pain and arthralgia, with hematuria; it does not cause oral ulcers or a facial rash.
C. Behcet: recurrent painful oral AND genital ulcers with uveitis, pathergy and erythema nodosum; glomerulonephritis with proteinuria is not typical.
D. Granulomatosis polyangitis: sinus/nasal disease (epistaxis, sinusitis), lung nodules or hemorrhage and renal disease, C-ANCA positive; a facial rash with oral ulcers and arthralgia in a young woman favors SLE.
key_concept:
SLE criteria: SOAP BRAIN MD.
  • Serositis, Oral ulcers, Arthritis, Photosensitivity.
  • Blood disorders, Renal (proteinuria, casts), ANA, Immunologic (anti dsDNA, anti Smith).
  • Neurologic, Malar rash, Discoid rash.
  • Screening: ANA (sensitive); specific: anti dsDNA, anti Smith.
  • Active nephritis: low C3/C4, high anti dsDNA.
exam_pearl: Young woman + oral ulcers + facial rash + arthritis + proteinuria = SLE; add genital ulcers and uveitis to think Behcet.

stem: Pancystolic murmur at the abex radiates to the axilla (ecg provided) what the Dx
highlight_terms_source: Pancystolic murmur at the abex radiates to the axilla
why_right: A "pansystolic murmur at the apex" that "radiates to the axilla" is the textbook murmur of mitral regurgitation. The ECG may show left atrial enlargement or atrial fibrillation from the volume loaded left atrium.
why_wrong_block:
B. MS: a mid diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap, not a systolic murmur.
C. AR: an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border, heard best leaning forward.
D. AS: a crescendo decrescendo ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, not the axilla.
key_concept:
Step 1: systolic or diastolic; step 2: site and radiation.
  • Apical pansystolic to axilla: MR.
  • Left lower sternal pansystolic, louder on inspiration: TR.
  • Ejection systolic to carotids: AS.
  • Early diastolic, left sternal edge: AR.
  • Mid diastolic rumble with opening snap: MS.
  • New murmur: TTE first.
exam_pearl: Radiation decides it: axilla = MR, carotids = AS.

stem: 64yo male with persistent a-fib, he also has HTN and DM, with no contraindications to antithrombotic therapy, what is the best medication for his case?
why_right: In "persistent a-fib", stroke risk is scored with CHA2DS2-VASc: hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 2; age 64 adds nothing yet. A score of 2 or more in a man means oral anticoagulation, and with "no contraindications" warfarin is the only anticoagulant offered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspirin and clopidogrel: dual antiplatelet therapy is less effective than anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention and bleeds about as much; it is used after ACS or stenting, not for AF.
B. Aspirin: antiplatelet monotherapy does not adequately prevent AF related stroke and is no longer recommended for this purpose.
C. Clopidogrel: same problem as aspirin; antiplatelets are not stroke prevention in AF when CHA2DS2-VASc is 2 or more.
key_concept:
AF stroke prevention by CHA2DS2-VASc.
  • C: heart failure 1; H: hypertension 1; A2: age ≥75 2; D: diabetes 1.
  • S2: stroke/TIA 2; V: vascular disease 1; A: age 65 to 74 1; Sc: female 1.
  • Men ≥2 (women ≥3): anticoagulate.
  • Men 1 (women 2): consider anticoagulation.
  • DOACs preferred over warfarin in non valvular AF; warfarin for mechanical valves or moderate to severe MS.
exam_pearl: Antiplatelets are never the answer for AF stroke prevention; if a DOAC is listed it beats warfarin in non valvular AF.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with episodic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits that have been present intermittently for the past year. The pain is "crampy." and moderate to severe. Defecation brings some relief, but she sometimes must pass several loose, watery stools before the pain resolves. She occasionally notes mucus in her stool and sometimes feels that evacuation is incomplete even though she is unable to pass more stool. Her body weight is stable. Abdominal examination are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to establish diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: episodic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits
why_right: Crampy pain for a year with "altered bowel habits", relief with defecation, mucus and incomplete evacuation, "stable" weight and a normal exam is irritable bowel syndrome (diarrhea predominant). IBS is diagnosed after excluding organic mimics, and celiac serology is the recommended test because celiac disease can produce identical symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Helicobacter pylori test: used for dyspepsia or peptic ulcer symptoms (epigastric pain, bloating), not lower abdominal pain with altered bowel habits.
C. Thyroid function test: not part of the routine IBS exclusion workup; check it only when there are features of thyroid disease (weight change, tremor, palpitations, cold intolerance).
D. CT abdomen: reserved for alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, anemia, older age, palpable mass); it is unnecessary in a young patient with typical IBS.
key_concept:
IBS: pain relieved by defecation + altered bowel habit; diagnose after limited exclusion tests.
  • CBC (anemia, infection).
  • CRP and fecal calprotectin (rule out IBD).
  • Celiac serology (tTG IgA).
  • Stool test for Giardia if diarrhea.
  • Red flags needing colonoscopy: blood in stool, nocturnal diarrhea, weight loss, anemia, age >50.
exam_pearl: Young patient with typical IBS and no red flags: celiac serology, not imaging or endoscopy.

stem: A patient with a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia presents with a 4-hour history of slurred speech. What is the target of LDL level?
why_right: "4-hour history of slurred speech" in a patient with hypertension and dyslipidemia is an ischemic stroke, which counts as clinical atherosclerotic disease and needs high intensity statin therapy. Secondary prevention after ischemic stroke aims for a low LDL (AHA/ASA: below 1.8 mmol/L, i.e. <70 mg/dL; European guidance is even lower), so "less than 2" is the strictest and therefore the correct choice among these options.
why_wrong_block:
B. Less than 2.2: above the recommended target after ischemic stroke; too lenient for a patient with established atherosclerotic disease.
C. Less than 2.5: an older or lower risk style target (around 100 mg/dL); not enough after a stroke.
D. Less than 3: a target for low to moderate risk primary prevention, not for secondary prevention after stroke.
key_concept:
Stroke/TIA of atherosclerotic origin = clinical ASCVD: high intensity statin, LDL <1.8 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL).
  • Clinical ASCVD (MI, stroke, TIA, PAD): high intensity statin.
  • LDL ≥190 mg/dL: high intensity statin.
  • Diabetes aged 40 to 75: moderate or high intensity by risk.
  • Conversion: mmol/L × 38.7 = mg/dL.
  • Add ezetimibe if target not reached on maximal statin.
exam_pearl: After stroke, pick the lowest LDL target offered; the higher numbers are primary prevention targets.

stem: Copd patient came with symptoms of pneumonia and the stem asked about most appropriate initial investigation for him ?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the most appropriate initial investigation for suspected pneumonia. Pneumonia is a radiological diagnosis, so a chest X-ray is the first test: it confirms consolidation, separates pneumonia from a simple COPD exacerbation or pneumothorax, and shows complications such as effusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood gas assesses severity (hypoxemia, CO2 retention) in a COPD patient and guides oxygen, but it does not diagnose pneumonia; it is done alongside, not instead of, imaging.
C. Blood or sputum/urine cultures (and urinary antigens) identify the organism in moderate to severe or admitted pneumonia, but results are delayed and they do not establish the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspected pneumonia: confirm with chest X-ray first.
  • CXR: diagnosis (consolidation) and complications
  • ABG: severity and type 2 respiratory failure in COPD
  • Cultures: organism, for admitted or severe cases
  • CBC/CRP: supportive, non-specific
exam_pearl: "Initial investigation" to diagnose = CXR; "assess severity / need for ventilation" in COPD = ABG.

stem: A female on warfarin presents with bloody stool, is pale, hypotensive, and has cool extremities. Her lab results show: Hb = 6 g/dL; PT and PTT prolonged; BP = 90/65. What is the initial step in fluid management?
why_right: This recall's key is PCC because the patient is on warfarin with a major bleed (bloody stool, hypotension, cool extremities) and prolonged PT/PTT. Warfarin with active bleeding requires urgent reversal with IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (or FFP if PCC is unavailable); PCC works fastest and in a small volume, so the source treats correcting the coagulopathy as the first step to stop ongoing loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ringer's lactate is a crystalloid for initial volume resuscitation; it restores volume but does not reverse the warfarin coagulopathy driving the bleed.
C. Normal saline is the first resuscitation fluid in an unstable GI bleed without coagulopathy (e.g. NSAID ulcer); here bleeding continues until warfarin is reversed.
D. Packed RBCs will also be needed (Hb 6 with shock) and replace oxygen-carrying capacity, but they do not reverse the warfarin effect that keeps her bleeding; this recall puts reversal first.
key_concept:
Warfarin + bleeding: admit, IV vitamin K + PCC (or FFP).
  • Bleeding on warfarin: IV vitamin K plus PCC (preferred) or FFP
  • No bleeding, INR above 10: hold warfarin, oral vitamin K
  • No bleeding, INR 4 to 10: hold warfarin, consider low-dose oral vitamin K
  • Unstable GI bleed: crystalloid resuscitation
  • Transfuse RBCs if Hb below 7 (below 8 with cardiac disease)
exam_pearl: Same shocked GI bleeder NOT on anticoagulants with Hb above 7 = normal saline; on warfarin = reverse with PCC + vitamin K.

stem: 76-year-old man, known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, presented to the clinic with exertional shortness of breath for 1 year. He has to slow down his walk and stop after 10 meters. He denied any history of syncope, chest pain, or palpitation. Precordium examination revealed a forceful apex beat and a crescendo- decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: crescendo- decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid
why_right: A crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid is the signature of aortic stenosis. The forceful (heaving) apex reflects concentric LVH from pressure overload, and the age (76) with diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidemia fits calcific degenerative AS. Exertional dyspnea is one of the classic AS symptoms (with angina and syncope), signalling severe disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mitral stenosis gives a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex, not a systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.
C. Pulmonary stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur at the left 2nd intercostal space that increases with inspiration and does not radiate to the carotids; it is usually congenital in younger patients.
D. Aortic regurgitation is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge with a collapsing pulse, not a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur.
key_concept:
Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids = aortic stenosis.
  • Elderly with atherosclerotic risk factors → calcific AS; young → bicuspid valve
  • Signs: slow-rising pulse, heaving apex, soft S2
  • Symptoms: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope (severe disease)
  • Diagnosis: transthoracic echocardiography
  • Symptomatic severe AS → valve replacement
exam_pearl: Systolic + carotid radiation = AS; if the systolic murmur rises on standing/Valsalva and falls with handgrip, think HOCM instead.

stem: A 25 years old male presented with progressive SOB and wheezing. On auscultation: wheezy chest, no crackles. History of previous hospitalization and intubation last year. Was given systemic steroids but no benefit which of the following is the most appropriate rescue (something like that) drug
highlight_terms_source: History of previous hospitalization and intubation
key_concept:
Acute severe asthma ladder: O2 → SABA → SAMA → systemic steroid → reassess/ICU → IV MgSO4 → intubation.
  • SABA: best bronchodilator
  • Systemic steroid: needed, but slow, not the rescue
  • IV MgSO4: refractory attack
  • Deteriorating after MgSO4: intubate
  • Previous intubation = high-risk, ICU
exam_pearl: "Given steroids but no benefit" + "rescue" points to the step after steroids (IV MgSO4); "already given MgSO4, still worse" = intubation.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Middle age pt with migraine headaches Ask about medication What medication is used for acute attacks ??
key_concept:
Headache: acute vs prophylaxis.
  • Migraine acute: mild/moderate NSAIDs, moderate/severe triptan
  • Migraine prophylaxis: beta blocker (propranolol)
  • Cluster acute: 100% oxygen; prophylaxis verapamil
  • Tension acute: NSAIDs; prophylaxis amitriptyline
exam_pearl: Triptans are contraindicated in ischemic heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension; then use NSAIDs.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 22 year old woman presented to the clinic with 2 months history of polyarthralgia, skin rash, mucosal ulcers and Fatigue. Her clinical examinations revealed malar rash over her face and active arthritis at several joints. Hb 100 (120-160 g/L female); Platelets count 100 (150-400) ×109/L; WBC 3 (4.5-10.5 ×109/L); ESR 35 (2-10 mm/h female); Lupus anticoagulant positive; Urea 5 (2.75-7.4 mmol/L); Creatinine 78 (44-115 umol/L); C-reactive peptide 5 (<8.2 mg/L); Complement C3 0.3 (0.7-1.5 g/L); Complement C4 0.13 (0.15-0.45 g/L). Which of the following test obtained at this visit is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is ANA. The young woman has a classic SLE picture: malar rash, mucosal ulcers, arthritis, pancytopenia, low C3/C4 and a positive lupus anticoagulant. ANA is positive in nearly all SLE patients, so it is the test used to establish the autoimmune basis; a negative ANA practically excludes SLE.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anti-Ro (SSA) is linked to Sjögren syndrome, subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus/congenital heart block; it is not the test that confirms systemic lupus.
C. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and tracks disease activity and nephritis, but it is negative in a sizeable share of patients, so it cannot exclude lupus; this recall keys the sensitive test, ANA.
D. Anti-RNP confirms mixed connective tissue disease (SLE features overlapping with myositis, Raynaud, scleroderma); there is no myositis or overlap here.
key_concept:
SLE antibodies: ANA most sensitive, anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA most specific.
  • ANA: most sensitive, screening; negative ANA practically excludes SLE
  • Anti-Sm: most specific
  • Anti-dsDNA: specific, activity and nephritis
  • Low C3/C4: activity, nephritis
  • Anti-histone: drug-induced lupus
  • Anti-Ro/La: neonatal lupus, Sjögren
exam_pearl: "Most sensitive / screening" = ANA; "most specific" = anti-Sm (then anti-dsDNA); SLE plus myositis overlap = anti-RNP.

stem: abdominal pain after meals no medical surgical or family history Next step in investigation:
key_concept:
Dyspepsia: age and red flags decide.
  • Young, no red flags: H. pylori test and treat
  • Red flags or older age at onset: urgent endoscopy
  • Barium study: dysphagia or EGD not possible
  • CT: complications, pancreatic or mesenteric causes
exam_pearl: Anemia or isolated high urea with normal creatinine (GI bleed) turns the same dyspepsia stem into endoscopy.

stem: male elderly with diabetes, on follow up not adhere to medx bc he is not believing in medx what to do?
OptA: explain diabetes and lifestyle by simple visual diagrams
key_concept:
Non-adherence from disbelief: explore beliefs, explain simply, build trust.
  • Use lay language, no jargon
  • Visual aids help low literacy and older patients
  • Written material only reinforces verbal teaching
  • Shared decision making improves compliance
exam_pearl: The answer that spends time with the patient (explain, check understanding, gain trust) usually beats a passive handout.

stem: Pt Newly dignosed with diabetes mellitus, Hb1C 7.9. His BMI 34. What is the first line for him?
why_right: A newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic with HbA1c 7.9 and BMI 34 starts lifestyle modification plus metformin. Metformin is first-line: effective, weight-neutral, no hypoglycemia, cheap. An HbA1c between 7.5 and 10% at diagnosis justifies starting it with lifestyle advice rather than lifestyle alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral add-on agents (or used when metformin is not tolerated or eGFR is low); they are not first line.
B. Liraglutide (GLP-1 agonist) is an injectable add-on, favoured with established cardiovascular disease or when weight loss is a priority after metformin; it is not first-line monotherapy.
D. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia and weight gain, a poor choice in an obese patient; they are second-line add-ons.
key_concept:
New T2DM: lifestyle + metformin.
  • HbA1c below 7.5%: lifestyle first
  • 7.5 to 10%: lifestyle plus metformin
  • Above 10% or symptomatic catabolic: insulin
  • Stop metformin if eGFR below 30
  • ASCVD/HF/CKD: add GLP-1 agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_pearl: Gestational diabetes = diet first; hospitalized patient = insulin, not oral agents.

stem: 28-year-old woman, not known to have any medical illness, complains of increased sleepiness, fatigue and does not drink alcohol. Examination reveals an overweight patient, not in distress, with no lymphadenopathy or masses (see lab results). high tsh, low t4 (dont remember numbers) +ve anti tpo. HBsag -ve. Anti hbs +ve. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Sleepiness, fatigue, overweight in a young woman with high TSH, low T4 is primary hypothyroidism, and positive anti-TPO confirms autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, the commonest cause in iodine-sufficient areas. HBsAg negative with anti-HBs positive just means hepatitis B immunity, a distractor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Graves' disease causes hyperthyroidism (low TSH, high T4, TSH-receptor antibodies), not hypothyroid symptoms.
B. Subacute thyroiditis presents with a painful tender thyroid and transient thyrotoxicosis after a viral illness, with high ESR; not a painless hypothyroid picture.
C. Sick euthyroid syndrome needs an acute non-thyroidal illness (ICU, sepsis) and shows low T3 with normal or low TSH; this woman has no illness and a high TSH.
key_concept:
High TSH + low T4 + anti-TPO = Hashimoto.
  • Hashimoto: hypothyroid, anti-TPO, painless
  • Graves: low TSH, TRAb, diffuse uptake
  • Subacute: painful, high ESR, low uptake
  • Sick euthyroid: low T3, acute illness
exam_pearl: Anti-TPO can also be positive early in Hashimoto with a transient hyperthyroid phase; the high TSH here settles it.

stem: An elderly patient presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and hypotension. On examination, there is a systolic murmur radiating to the axilla. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V2–V4, and troponin is markedly elevated. What is the most likely cause of hypotension?
highlight_terms_source: systolic murmur radiating to the axilla
why_right: After an acute STEMI (ST elevation V2 to V4, high troponin), a new systolic murmur radiating to the axilla with hypotension means acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture. The question asks for the cause of hypotension, and the murmur identifies the mechanism: sudden regurgitant volume drops forward cardiac output and floods the lungs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardiogenic shock describes the hemodynamic state, not its cause; the axillary-radiating murmur names the specific mechanism (acute MR).
B. Pulmonary embolism gives sudden dyspnea and hypotension with right heart strain (S1Q3T3, RBBB), not anterior ST elevation and an MR murmur.
C. Drug-induced hypotension (nitrates, morphine, beta blockers) is possible after MI but would not produce a new murmur radiating to the axilla.
key_concept:
Post-MI new murmur + shock: find the mechanism.
  • Apical pansystolic to axilla + pulmonary edema: papillary muscle rupture/acute MR
  • Harsh parasternal systolic + thrill, step-up in O2: VSD
  • Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds: free wall rupture/tamponade
  • Papillary rupture typically 2 to 7 days, more with inferior MI
exam_pearl: Murmur to axilla = MR; loud harsh murmur at left sternal border with thrill = ventricular septal rupture.

stem: 42 Y. O women taking chemotherapy for breast cancer, come in flu season and ask for vaccines due her weak immunity. What vaccine to give and which type
OptD: Avoid all vaccine untill complete chemotherapy
key_concept:
Immunosuppressed patient: inactivated vaccines YES, live vaccines NO.
  • Inactivated (killed) influenza injection: safe, cannot cause flu
  • Live attenuated: intranasal flu, MMR, varicella, zoster live, yellow fever: avoid
  • Live vaccines deferred until immune recovery (e.g., at least 1 month off high dose steroids)
  • Response to vaccine may be reduced during chemo, but benefit still outweighs risk
exam_pearl: Immunocompromised does not mean no vaccines; it means no LIVE vaccines.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with altered sensorium for the last 2 days and headaches for 5 days, with a history of fever for the preceding month. On examination, there is nuchal rigidity (see lab results). Hb 100 (130-170 g/L); WBC 11 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L); Glucose, fasting 7.22 (3.5-6.5 mmol/L). Cerebrospinal Fluid: Appearance turbid (clear); Cells 240 (0-3 /uL); Total protein 3.6 (0.22-0.33 g/L); Glucose 2.7 (2.50-3.89 mmol/L); Neutrophils 23%; Lymphocytes 73%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: history of fever for the preceding month
why_right: A month of fever before meningitis signs points to a subacute cause, classically TB. The CSF shows lymphocyte predominance (73%) with very high protein (3.6 g/L) and glucose 2.7 that is low relative to serum glucose 7.22 (ratio below 0.5). Lymphocytes plus low glucose plus high protein in a subacute course = tubercular meningitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Septicemia: does not explain nuchal rigidity with a lymphocytic, high protein CSF; it would be right for systemic sepsis without CSF meningitis findings.
C. Pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis: acute (hours to days) with neutrophil predominant CSF and very low glucose; here the course is a month and lymphocytes dominate.
D. Viral meningoencephalitis: acute course with lymphocytes but normal glucose and only mildly raised protein; not a month of fever with protein this high.
key_concept:
Read CSF by cell type + glucose (compare with serum).
  • Neutrophils + low glucose: bacterial
  • Lymphocytes + low glucose + high protein: TB (or fungal)
  • Lymphocytes + normal glucose: viral
  • CSF/serum glucose ratio below 0.5 = low
exam_pearl: A 'normal' CSF glucose number can still be low if the serum glucose is high; always calculate the ratio.

stem: pt symptomatic came to er, pic provided with heart block, what to do to diagnose (not sure tho)?
why_right: In a symptomatic patient in the ER with a new heart block, an ischemic cause (especially inferior MI involving the right coronary artery, which supplies the AV node) must be excluded. Invasive coronary angiography is the definitive test to diagnose coronary occlusion and allows treatment in the same sitting, so the recall keys it as the diagnostic step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocardial perfusion scan: a non-invasive test for stable patients with suspected chronic ischemia; not appropriate for an acutely symptomatic ER patient.
B. Coronary CT angiogram: suits low to intermediate risk stable chest pain to rule out CAD; it cannot treat a lesion and is less suitable in an unstable patient with conduction disease.
D. Chest X-ray: gives no information on coronary anatomy or the cause of the block; useful only for complications such as pulmonary edema.
key_concept:
Heart block on ECG: recognise degree, stabilise, then find the cause.
  • 1st degree: long PR, no dropped beats
  • 2nd degree: some P waves not followed by QRS
  • 3rd degree: P and QRS independent (AV dissociation)
  • Unstable bradycardia: atropine, then pacing
  • Suspected ischemic cause (inferior MI/RCA): coronary angiography
exam_pearl: The recall itself is uncertain: if the question asks for treatment of unstable complete heart block, the answer shifts to atropine/pacing, not a diagnostic test.

stem: male in his 50s, smoker complaining of cough with clear mucus and breathlessness. This attack lasted for 3-4 days and similar attacks 1 year ago. Chest x ray hyperinflation (not sure what else). Diagnosis?
key_concept:
How to decide in a smoker with recurrent cough and breathlessness:
  • Chronic bronchitis: productive cough at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years
  • Emphysema: barrel chest, hyperresonance, air trapping/hyperinflation
  • Bronchiectasis: large volumes of purulent sputum, clubbing, HRCT tram tracks
  • Cancer: hemoptysis, weight loss, mass or collapse on X-ray
  • PE: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxia, often clear X-ray
  • Spirometry is the diagnostic test for COPD
exam_pearl: Large volumes of purulent sputum with clubbing point to bronchiectasis rather than chronic bronchitis.

stem: A patient presents with signs & symptoms of meningitis. Lumbar puncture findings are as follows: CSF glucose: 3.5mmol/L, CSF protein: 500 mg/L (reference range: 100–400 mg/L), Predominant lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the specific causative organism?
why_right: The CSF shows predominant lymphocytes, normal glucose (3.5 mmol/L) and only mildly raised protein (500 mg/L), which is a viral pattern. When the LP result is given, treat according to it: the treatable viral cause to cover is herpes simplex, so IV acyclovir is the specific therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone and vancomycin: the bacterial meningitis regimen, right with neutrophil predominant CSF, low glucose and high protein; not a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.
B. IV methylprednisolone: steroids (dexamethasone) are an adjunct in bacterial meningitis, and high dose methylprednisolone is for relapses of demyelinating disease; neither treats a viral organism.
C. Antifungal therapy: right for cryptococcal meningitis, typically in immunocompromised (HIV) patients with lymphocytes and LOW glucose; no such clue here.
key_concept:
If the CSF result is given, treat the organism it points to, not the empirical cocktail.
  • Neutrophils + low glucose: ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • Lymphocytes + normal glucose: viral, IV acyclovir (HSV)
  • Lymphocytes + low glucose: TB (or fungal if immunocompromised)
  • Unknown CSF, sick patient: empirical ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone + acyclovir
exam_pearl: Confusion, seizures or temporal lobe changes with a lymphocytic CSF = HSV encephalitis; acyclovir should never be delayed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: version: 22-year-old man, 4 days fever, headache, confusion, Kernig's sign, T 39, CSF cells 380, protein 0.8, glucose 3.7, 90% lymphocytes, culture pending; options Ceftriaxone+vancomycin+steroid / Ceftriaxone+vancomycin / Ceftriaxone / Acyclovir, Acyclovir highlighted. Screenshot on next page (4 year old, convulsion, decreased LOC, viral illness few days ago, clear CSF, normal protein, lymphocytosis, low glucose): A- Acyclovir (HSV encephalitis); normal protein and clear CSF favor HSV over TB; 25% of HSV cases have low CSF glucose.

stem: Patient is planning a long flight. He is concerned about developing deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measure?
OptA: Keep legs elevated throughout the flight
OptC: Perform periodic leg exercises and ambulate during the flight
why_right: For a traveller on a long flight, the recommended general prevention is to keep the calf muscle pump active: periodic leg/calf exercises, walking in the aisle when possible, and staying hydrated. This reduces venous stasis, the main mechanism of travel related DVT.
why_wrong_block:
A. Keeping legs elevated throughout the flight is impractical and does not replace muscle activity; prolonged immobility in any position promotes stasis.
B. Aspirin is not recommended for travel DVT prophylaxis; in selected high risk travellers (prior VTE, recent surgery, active cancer) compression stockings or LMWH are considered instead.
key_concept:
Long haul travel DVT prevention by risk level:
  • All travellers: calf exercises, walk periodically, aisle seat, hydration, avoid tight clothing and sedatives
  • Higher risk: properly fitted below knee compression stockings
  • Very high risk: LMWH may be considered individually
  • Aspirin: not recommended for this purpose
exam_pearl: Aspirin is the tempting 'drug' option, but for travel DVT the answer is mobilisation, not antiplatelets.

stem: X-ray (image) with lower lobe involvement. What is the most likely organism?
why_right: A focal lobar (lower lobe) consolidation on X-ray is the typical pneumonia pattern, and Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community acquired lobar pneumonia. Without other clues pointing elsewhere, the 'most likely organism' is pneumococcus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staphylococcus aureus: suspect after influenza, in IV drug users or with cavitating/multiple lesions and abscesses; not the default for a single lobar consolidation.
B. Mycoplasma: atypical pneumonia in young people with dry cough and bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates, not a dense lobar consolidation.
C. Legionella: suspect with severe pneumonia plus diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia or exposure to water systems/air conditioning; the X-ray alone does not point to it.
key_concept:
Typical (lobar) vs atypical (interstitial) pneumonia:
  • Typical: productive cough, fever, lobar consolidation; most common S. pneumoniae
  • Atypical: dry cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates; Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, viruses
  • Post influenza or cavitation: S. aureus
  • GI symptoms, hyponatremia: Legionella
  • Foul sputum, aspiration risk: anaerobes
exam_pearl: Bilateral interstitial pattern with dry cough switches the answer from pneumococcus to Mycoplasma.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall mentions an X-ray image (not shown on page).

stem: A patient presented with green sputum and fever. The chest X-ray shows consolidation. What is the most likely cause?
key_concept:
Pick the organism from the extra clue, otherwise pneumococcus.
  • No special clue: Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Water exposure, GI symptoms, hyponatremia: Legionella
  • Young, dry cough, bilateral infiltrates: Mycoplasma
  • Post influenza, cavitation: Staph aureus
exam_pearl: Sputum colour does not identify the organism; look for an exposure or extrapulmonary clue (water systems, diarrhea, hyponatremia) before moving away from pneumococcus.

stem: Patient has mycoplasma infection with low Hb.
why_right: Mycoplasma can cause immune mediated hemolysis (cold agglutinins), explaining the low Hb. This recall's key is corticosteroids on the reasoning that the anemia is autoimmune, so immunosuppression is chosen over doing nothing.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance is the source's distractor on the basis that the hemolysis needs active treatment; it would be right for mild, transient post Mycoplasma hemolysis managed by treating the infection and keeping the patient warm.
key_concept:
Warm vs cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia:
  • Warm: IgG, Coombs IgG ± C3, spherocytes; causes autoimmune disease, lymphoma; treatment corticosteroids first line
  • Cold: IgM, Coombs C3 only, agglutination; causes Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoproliferative; treatment keep warm, treat cause, plasmapheresis if severe
  • Mycoplasma hemolysis is usually transient
exam_pearl: Steroids treat WARM (IgG) AIHA; Mycoplasma gives COLD (IgM) agglutinin hemolysis, which responds poorly to steroids.

stem: (21 years age) present with knee pain and mild fever and systolic murmur after 3 weeks of URTI. What gives?
key_concept:
Acute rheumatic fever: Jones criteria after group A strep pharyngitis (typically 2 to 4 weeks later).
  • All patients: penicillin to eradicate strep, then secondary prophylaxis
  • Arthritis and mild carditis: aspirin (high dose NSAID)
  • Severe carditis / heart failure: corticosteroids, plus diuretics
  • Echocardiography to assess carditis
  • Prophylaxis without carditis: 5 years or to age 21, whichever is longer
  • Carditis without residual disease: 10 years or to age 21, whichever is longer
exam_pearl: Fever + migratory large joint arthritis + new murmur weeks after a sore throat = rheumatic fever: aspirin for joints, steroids only if carditis is severe, penicillin for everyone.

stem: A 45-year-old man under investigation for hypertension was prescribed a drug for his lipid disorder. One week later, he returned with intense facial flushing after taking the medication. He was advised to take a full dose of aspirin three times daily instead of a low dose once daily, which completely relieved the flushing. [HDL 0.72 mmol/L (<1.03), LDL 5.30 mmol/L (<3.36), total cholesterol 6.12 mmol/L (<5.1), triglycerides 2.20 mmol/L (<2.16); ALT 35 IU/L (5-40), CK 205 IU/L (24-195)] Which drug was he prescribed?
why_right: Intense facial flushing within a week of starting a lipid drug that is relieved by aspirin is the signature of niacin (nicotinic acid). The flush is prostaglandin mediated (mainly PGD2), so a cyclooxygenase inhibitor like aspirin taken beforehand prevents it. Niacin also suits this profile: it is the most potent HDL raiser and lowers LDL and triglycerides, matching his low HDL with high LDL.
why_wrong_block:
B. Clofibrate: a fibrate whose typical effects are gallstones, myopathy (especially with statins) and GI upset, not prostaglandin flushing. Right when the question features a drug for severe hypertriglyceridemia.
C. Atorvastatin: causes myalgia/myopathy and raised transaminases, not flushing that aspirin abolishes. Right when the stem describes muscle pain or a rising CK on a lipid drug.
D. Cholestyramine: a bile acid sequestrant causing bloating, constipation, raised triglycerides and reduced absorption of other drugs and fat-soluble vitamins. Right when the side effect is GI or malabsorptive.
key_concept:
Match the lipid drug to its signature side effect.
  • Niacin: flushing (prevented by aspirin), hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia/gout, hepatotoxicity
  • Statins: myopathy, raised transaminases
  • Fibrates: gallstones, myopathy with statins
  • Bile acid sequestrants: GI upset, raised TG, reduced drug and fat-soluble vitamin absorption
  • Ezetimibe: generally well tolerated, mild diarrhea
exam_pearl: Flushing relieved by aspirin = niacin; the aspirin clue is the giveaway, not the lipid numbers.

stem: A 28-year-old patient presents with a history of 10-day of palpitations, sweating and neck discomfort. BP 110/70, HR 116, RR 18, temperature 37.7 C, SpO2 95%. Free T4 76.5 (8.5-15.2 pmol/L), TSH 0.15 (0.4-5.0), WBC 5.2, ESR 73 (2-10 mm/h). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Neck discomfort is the keyword for subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis. Combined with 10 days of thyrotoxic symptoms, low-grade fever (37.7 C), high free T4 (76.5), suppressed TSH (0.15) and a markedly raised ESR (73) with a normal WBC, the picture is an inflammatory, destructive thyroiditis rather than overproduction of hormone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Graves' disease: painless hyperthyroidism with diffuse goiter, eye signs and positive TSH receptor antibodies; ESR is normal. Right when there is a painless diffuse goiter or ophthalmopathy and high uptake on scan.
C. Hashimoto's thyroiditis: painless and usually presents with hypothyroidism (high TSH, fatigue, weight gain); it does not give a high ESR with neck pain.
D. Multinodular toxic goiter: painless hyperthyroidism in an older patient with a nodular goiter and patchy uptake; no neck pain, no raised ESR.
key_concept:
Thyrotoxicosis + painful/tender thyroid + high ESR = subacute thyroiditis.
  • Often follows an URTI; fever, malaise
  • Low TSH, high T4/T3, raised ESR
  • Radioactive iodine uptake: low (vs high in Graves)
  • Treatment: NSAIDs (steroids if severe) for pain, beta-blocker for symptoms
  • No antithyroid drugs: the problem is hormone leak, not synthesis
  • Course: hyper, then possible transient hypo, then usually normal
exam_pearl: Neck pain + thyrotoxicosis + high ESR: subacute thyroiditis, and do not reach for carbimazole.

stem: A 33-year-old man with a history of severe asthma is admitted to the Emergency Department with an asthma attack. He received high-flow oxygen and nebulized salbutamol. He is unable to complete sentences, has bilateral expiratory wheeze, and is unable to perform a peak flow reading. He was immediately given intravenous hydrocortisone and nebulized salbutamol continuously. After 10 minutes, there is no improvement, and intravenous magnesium sulfate was given. His condition continues to deteriorate (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: He has at least acute severe asthma (cannot complete sentences, too breathless to perform a peak flow) and has already received oxygen, continuous salbutamol, IV hydrocortisone and then IV magnesium sulfate, yet he "continues to deteriorate". Magnesium is the last medical step in the acute asthma ladder, so deterioration after it means securing the airway with intubation and mechanical ventilation (ICU).
why_wrong_block:
A. NIV is the rescue for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations in an alert patient; in deteriorating acute asthma it is not standard and only delays definitive airway control.
B. IV aminophylline is a senior or ICU option with a narrow therapeutic window and little added benefit; a patient deteriorating after magnesium needs ventilation, not another bronchodilator.
C. Nebulized ipratropium belongs early in the ladder alongside salbutamol; it would not rescue a patient who is still worsening after magnesium.
key_concept:
Acute severe asthma ladder (escalate when not improving):
  • Oxygen
  • Nebulized SABA (back to back if needed)
  • Add nebulized ipratropium
  • Systemic steroid (IV hydrocortisone or oral prednisolone)
  • IV magnesium sulfate, involve ICU
  • Still deteriorating: intubate and ventilate
exam_pearl: Asthma worsening after IV magnesium = intubate; COPD with hypercapnic acidosis in an alert patient = NIV.

stem: Elderly patient who recently underwent major surgery is now presenting with shortness of breath, chest pain, and has a confirmed DVT. The patient also had an ischemic stroke two months ago. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Breathlessness and chest pain with a confirmed DVT after recent major surgery means venous thromboembolism, most likely PE. The key is the bleeding profile: recent major surgery plus an ischemic stroke two months ago is read by this question as a contraindication to anticoagulation and an absolute bar to fibrinolysis (stroke within 3 months). When DVT/PE coexists with a contraindication to anticoagulation, an IVC filter is placed to stop further emboli reaching the lungs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Start warfarin: warfarin is never started alone in acute VTE (slow onset and an early prothrombotic phase) and needs heparin/LMWH overlap; here anticoagulation is considered contraindicated anyway. Right as long-term therapy after LMWH in a patient who can be anticoagulated.
C. Administer fibrinolytics: reserved for massive PE with shock, and ischemic stroke within 3 months and recent major surgery are contraindications. Right when PE causes hypotension and there is no bleeding contraindication.
key_concept:
PE / DVT management by circulation and bleeding risk.
  • Stable, no contraindication: heparin or LMWH, then oral anticoagulant
  • Stable, anticoagulation contraindicated: IVC filter
  • Recurrent emboli despite adequate anticoagulation: IVC filter
  • Massive PE (shock): thrombolysis
  • Massive PE with thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: embolectomy
exam_pearl: If LMWH/heparin is offered and there is no real bleeding contraindication, it beats a filter; the filter is the answer only when the stem makes anticoagulation unsafe, as here.

stem: 26 yo man, complaining of intermittent wheezing after exercise, he mentioned he always gets wheezing after exercising, on exam diffuse bilateral wheeze. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A young man with intermittent wheezing after exercise that he always gets, and diffuse bilateral wheeze, has exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. The inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist salbutamol is the reliever: it relaxes bronchial smooth muscle within minutes and is also taken shortly before exercise to prevent attacks. Nothing in the stem suggests a severe attack needing IV therapy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Inhaler fluticasone: an inhaled steroid controller with no immediate bronchodilator effect. Right when asthma is persistent (frequent reliever use, night waking) and needs regular controller therapy.
C. IV Mg: reserved for acute severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to nebulized bronchodilators and steroids.
D. IV steroid: systemic steroids are for moderate to severe exacerbations (oral usually suffices); not for a mild, intermittent exercise-triggered wheeze.
key_concept:
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: SABA (salbutamol) as reliever and before exercise.
  • Step 1 mild intermittent: SABA as needed
  • Persistent symptoms: add regular low-dose ICS (controller)
  • Uncontrolled on ICS: add LABA; never LABA alone
  • Acute severe attack: oxygen, nebulized SABA, ipratropium, systemic steroid, then IV Mg if poor response
  • Current GINA discourages SABA-only treatment for ongoing asthma; frequent symptoms warrant an ICS-containing regimen
exam_pearl: Wheeze triggered by exercise = salbutamol before exercise; IV magnesium and IV steroids belong to the severe attack, not this one.

stem: A 30-40 man getting blood transfusion in the ER and minutes after he got skin rash and facial flushes. How to prevent this?
OptD: Matching the recipient with the donor ethnicity
why_right: Skin rash and facial flushing starting minutes after a transfusion is a mild allergic (urticarial) reaction to donor plasma proteins, mediated by histamine release. For a patient who has had such reactions, pre-medication with an antihistamine before future transfusions is the preventive step this recall keys.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pushing the bag quickly does nothing to prevent allergy and risks circulatory overload; a slow rate is used to prevent TACO.
C. Warming blood prevents hypothermia and arrhythmias in rapid or massive transfusion, not allergic skin reactions.
D. Donor ethnicity is irrelevant; compatibility depends on ABO/Rh and antibody screening, and these do not prevent plasma-protein allergic reactions.
key_concept:
Transfusion reactions and prevention:
  • Urticaria, flushing, itch: allergic; antihistamine (premedicate next time)
  • Anaphylaxis (IgA deficiency): washed or IgA-deficient products
  • Fever, chills (febrile non-hemolytic): leukoreduced blood, antipyretic
  • Fever, hypotension, hemoglobinuria: acute hemolytic (ABO mismatch); stop transfusion
  • Rapid or massive transfusion: blood warmer
exam_pearl: Rash only, stable vitals: pause, give antihistamine, may resume; add hypotension or wheeze and it is anaphylaxis, stop and give adrenaline.
