stem: 35-year-old male with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and weight loss. Endoscopy: blunting of villi. Diagnosis:
why_right: Chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea and weight loss describe small bowel malabsorption, and blunting of villi (villous atrophy) on duodenal biopsy is the hallmark of celiac disease. The full histology is villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes; treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.
why_wrong_block:
B. Whipple's disease: also causes malabsorption, but biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria, usually in a middle-aged man with arthralgia, fever and neurological signs. Right when the stem mentions PAS-positive macrophages or Tropheryma whipplei.
C. Crohn's disease: transmural inflammation with skip lesions, aphthous/deep ulcers, strictures and non-caseating granulomas, often terminal ileum with RLQ pain, fistulas or perianal disease. Villous blunting is not its defining finding.
key_concept:
Malabsorption + villous atrophy = celiac disease.
  • Screen: IgA tTG (check total IgA)
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy on gluten (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • Associations: type 1 DM, dermatitis herpetiformis, iron deficiency
  • Treatment: gluten-free diet
  • Whipple: PAS-positive macrophages
  • Crohn: granulomas, skip lesions, transmural
exam_pearl: Blunted villi = celiac; foamy PAS-positive macrophages = Whipple; granulomas = Crohn.

stem: Question about old male with hyperlipidemia and hypertension on medication. He came with progressive abdominal distention. He had AST elevated months ago, and now he came with progressive abdominal distention. No other symptoms were mentioned. Labs, AST and ALT were high, almost 100 both. Asking what is the best next step or image.
highlight_terms_source: AST and ALT were high, almost 100 both
why_right: An older man with hyperlipidemia and hypertension (metabolic risk), persistently raised AST/ALT (around 100, a mild chronic rise) and now progressive abdominal distention is most likely developing chronic liver disease (e.g. fatty liver progressing to cirrhosis) with ascites. The lead-in asks for the next step / imaging: abdominal ultrasound is the initial test, showing liver texture and size, ascites, splenomegaly and focal lesions, cheaply and without radiation. Biopsy is the confirmatory test later, not the first step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echo: right when ascites is suspected to be cardiac (raised JVP, edema, heart failure signs, high SAAG with high ascitic protein). The stem points to the liver via the long history of raised transaminases.
C. CT abdomen: not the first-line test; it follows ultrasound when a focal lesion needs characterizing (e.g. multiphasic CT for a nodule in a cirrhotic liver) or when ultrasound is inconclusive.
key_concept:
Suspected chronic liver disease or new ascites: ultrasound first.
  • Initial: abdominal ultrasound (liver, spleen, ascites, portal vein, focal lesions)
  • New ascites: also diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, protein, cell count)
  • Focal lesion over 1 cm in cirrhosis: multiphasic CT or MRI
  • Confirmatory / staging: liver biopsy (or elastography for fibrosis)
  • Cardiac cause suspected (raised JVP): echocardiography
exam_pearl: "Next step" or "initial imaging" for a liver problem = ultrasound; "best/gold/confirmatory" = biopsy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler note: Initial = US; BEST/GOLD/CONFIRMATORY = BIOPSY. (No option highlighted; the note endorses ultrasound as the initial step.) A separate 'Q:' version (60-year-old female, options incl. 'Ultrasound liver and spleen' highlighted) follows as its own card.

stem: A 60-year-old female with history of HTN, DLP, DM, came with increased abdominal distention, no history of alcohol use, he reported 10 years history of high aminotransferase, upon examination she has ascites no organomegaly. What is the next step? There were labs of elevated LFTS I think 3-fold NOT in the thousands but don't remember them unfortunately. And question asked for next step.
highlight_terms_source: elevated LFTS I think 3-fold NOT in the thousands
why_right: A 60-year-old with HTN, DLP and DM, no alcohol and a 10-year history of raised aminotransferases (mild, not in the thousands) now has ascites: this is the story of metabolic fatty liver disease progressing to cirrhosis. The next step is ultrasound of the liver and spleen to look for a cirrhotic liver, splenomegaly/portal hypertension, ascites and any focal lesion. Biopsy confirms and stages later; it is not the first move.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echocardiography: right when ascites may be from right heart failure or constrictive pericarditis (raised JVP, edema, cardiac history); here the decade of abnormal liver enzymes in a metabolic patient points to the liver.
C. Ct abdomen: second line after ultrasound, mainly to characterize a focal liver lesion (multiphasic CT) or when ultrasound is inconclusive.
D. Maybe liver biopsy: the gold standard to confirm and stage chronic liver disease, but it is invasive and comes after non-invasive imaging; ascites also increases its risk.
key_concept:
Metabolic risk factors + chronic mild transaminase rise + ascites = suspect MASLD/NAFLD cirrhosis.
  • Initial: ultrasound liver and spleen
  • New ascites: diagnostic paracentesis with SAAG
  • Fibrosis: elastography or non-invasive scores
  • Focal lesion over 1 cm in cirrhosis: multiphasic CT or MRI
  • Confirmatory / gold: liver biopsy
exam_pearl: Initial = ultrasound, gold = biopsy: read the lead-in verb before choosing.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 1277. Compiler note for the block: Initial = US; BEST/GOLD/CONFIRMATORY = BIOPSY.

stem: 50 years old man in the clinic with stressful job and high sodium diet and no physical activity bp: high (i guess it was 150/90? Im not sure) Sodium:high
OptB: ask him to monitor his bp and follow up
OptC: lifestyle changes (was more specific like less sodium and more activity)
OptD: tell him his bp is okay and nothing to worry about
highlight_terms_source: stressful job and high sodium diet and no physical activity
why_right: A 50-year-old with a high sodium diet, no physical activity and a stressful job has a mildly raised clinic BP (about 150/90, grade 1 range in ESC/WHO terms) with no organ damage, diabetes or cardiovascular disease mentioned. The first step is lifestyle modification targeted at his risk factors: salt restriction, regular aerobic exercise, weight control and stress reduction, with repeat measurements to confirm sustained hypertension before drugs are considered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Prescribed anti hypertensive immediately: right when BP is markedly high (grade 2 or more, e.g. ≥160/100), or with target organ damage, diabetes, CKD or established cardiovascular disease, or when lifestyle measures have failed.
B. Ask him to monitor his bp and follow up: confirming the reading is reasonable, but it misses the modifiable causes clearly planted in the stem; monitoring without advice is incomplete management.
D. Tell him his bp is okay and nothing to worry about: false reassurance; a BP around 150/90 is raised and needs action and follow up.
key_concept:
Mild hypertension, low risk: lifestyle first, then reassess.
  • Lifestyle: less salt, aerobic exercise, weight loss, DASH-style diet, limit alcohol, stop smoking
  • Confirm with repeated clinic, home or ambulatory readings
  • Drugs now: grade 2+ BP, organ damage, diabetes, CKD or high CV risk
  • Drugs later: lifestyle fails over a few months
  • Note: ACC/AHA calls ≥140/90 stage 2 and pairs lifestyle with a drug; ESC/NICE allow lifestyle first in low risk grade 1
exam_pearl: When the stem lists salt, inactivity and stress with mildly raised BP, the exam wants lifestyle change; drugs first only if BP is very high or there is organ damage or high risk.

stem: Pt came with cough and frothy pink sputum BP 80/40 HR 125 O2 (I think low) I think the question is asking what is true regarding the condition
why_right: Cough with frothy pink sputum means acute pulmonary edema, and with BP 80/40, HR 125 and hypoxia this is cardiogenic shock from a failing left ventricle. The body compensates for the low cardiac output with sympathetic vasoconstriction, so systemic vascular resistance rises (cold, clammy peripheries). An increased SVR is therefore the true statement.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardiac output is decreased in cardiogenic shock (the pump has failed). A high cardiac output is the pattern of distributive shock such as sepsis (warm peripheries, low SVR).
C. Central venous pressure is normal or raised in cardiogenic shock because blood backs up behind the failing heart. A low CVP fits hypovolemic or distributive shock.
D. PCWP is raised in cardiogenic shock; that high left sided filling pressure is exactly what pushes fluid into the alveoli and causes pink frothy sputum. Low PCWP is seen in hypovolemic, septic and neurogenic shock.
key_concept:
Shock hemodynamics: identify the type, then predict CO, PCWP and SVR.
  • Cardiogenic: CO low, PCWP HIGH, SVR high
  • Hypovolemic: CO low, PCWP low, SVR high
  • Septic: CO HIGH, PCWP low, SVR low
  • Neurogenic: CO low, HR LOW (bradycardia), SVR low
  • High PCWP points to cardiogenic; high CO points to distributive (septic) shock
exam_pearl: Pink frothy sputum + hypotension = cardiogenic shock: low CO, high PCWP, high SVR.

stem: 59 have fever chills copd , dm , we give fluid bolus and bp still low
highlight_terms_source: we give fluid bolus and bp still low
why_right: Fever and chills in a 59 year old with COPD and DM who stays hypotensive after a fluid bolus is fluid refractory septic shock. Once adequate fluid has failed to restore pressure, the next step is a vasopressor to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above, and norepinephrine is the first line vasopressor in septic shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Dobutamine is an inotrope for low cardiac output states (cardiogenic shock, or septic shock with myocardial dysfunction despite pressors). It can vasodilate and drop BP further, so it is not the first agent for distributive hypotension.
B. Hydrocortisone is added only for refractory septic shock that persists despite adequate fluids AND ongoing vasopressor therapy. It is not given before a vasopressor.
D. More fluid is right if the initial resuscitation volume has not yet been given and the patient is still fluid responsive. Here the stem says BP is still low after fluids, which is the trigger to start a vasopressor rather than keep loading (risk of pulmonary edema).
key_concept:
Septic shock ladder:
  • Step 1: crystalloid resuscitation + cultures + early antibiotics
  • Step 2: still hypotensive after fluids → norepinephrine (target MAP ≥ 65)
  • Step 3: rising pressor needs → add vasopressin
  • Step 4: refractory shock on pressors → hydrocortisone
  • Low cardiac output despite pressors → add dobutamine
exam_pearl: No fluids yet → fluids; fluids given and BP still low → norepinephrine.

stem: janduice and 2 Liver lesion in the right lobe what is the disease that is risk factor for this condition
highlight_terms_source: 2 Liver lesion in the right lobe
why_right: Jaundice with two right lobe liver lesions (classically in a nodular cirrhotic liver) is hepatocellular carcinoma until proven otherwise. The question asks for the risk factor, and chronic hepatitis B is the most common and strongest cause of HCC worldwide and in Saudi Arabia; it can cause HCC even without cirrhosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aflatoxin (Aspergillus contaminated grain) is a real HCC carcinogen and acts synergistically with HBV, but it is far less common than hepatitis B as the driving cause. It would be the answer only if the stem stressed moldy stored grain exposure.
B. Lead is not a recognised risk factor for HCC. Lead poisoning causes anemia with basophilic stippling, neuropathy and abdominal colic.
C. Wilson disease causes cirrhosis, but its HCC risk is low compared with viral hepatitis. Think Wilson in a young patient with liver disease, neuropsychiatric signs and Kayser Fleischer rings.
key_concept:
Liver mass in a cirrhotic liver = HCC; know the causes in order of importance.
  • Hepatitis B: most common cause, can cause HCC without cirrhosis
  • Hepatitis C, alcohol, NASH: via cirrhosis
  • Hemochromatosis: high HCC risk among metabolic causes
  • Aflatoxin: environmental carcinogen, synergistic with HBV
  • Diagnosis: multiphase (triphasic) CT/MRI ± AFP
exam_pearl: 'Strongest/most common risk factor for HCC' = hepatitis B, not aflatoxin or Wilson.

stem: Pt treat his rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate and have mouth ulcer and rigor what is the cause
why_right: The stem links the symptoms to the drug: a patient on methotrexate who develops mouth ulcers (mucositis) and rigors (infection). Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that causes bone marrow suppression and mucosal toxicity, so neutropenia with a febrile infection is the explanation. Management is to stop methotrexate, check a CBC, treat as febrile neutropenia and give folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue.
why_wrong_block: A. Felty syndrome also causes neutropenia with infections, but it needs long standing seropositive RA with splenomegaly (SANTA: splenomegaly, anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, arthritis). Nothing here points to it, while mouth ulcers in a patient taking methotrexate point to drug toxicity.
key_concept:
Neutropenia in an RA patient: drug toxicity vs Felty.
  • Methotrexate: mucositis/mouth ulcers, cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis
  • Toxicity worsens with renal impairment, folate deficiency, trimethoprim co prescription
  • Prevention: weekly dosing + folic acid; overdose/toxicity: folinic acid
  • Felty: long standing seropositive RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia
  • Other options a student may weigh: septic arthritis, opportunistic infection on immunosuppression
exam_pearl: Mouth ulcers + fever on methotrexate = marrow toxicity; Felty needs splenomegaly.

stem: women with MVP and sever MR without endocarditis , want dentist procedure what to give?
key_concept:
IE prophylaxis = high risk heart + high risk (dental) procedure.
  • High risk: prosthetic valve/material, prior IE, cyanotic or incompletely repaired CHD, transplant valvulopathy
  • NOT indicated: MVP with MR, acquired valve disease, bicuspid valve, ASD, HCM, rheumatic fever without prosthesis
  • Drug of choice: oral amoxicillin before the procedure (penicillin allergy: alternative such as azithromycin/clarithromycin or doxycycline)
  • Metronidazole is not an IE prophylaxis drug
exam_pearl: Severity of MR does not change the rule: native MVP/MR alone never earns prophylaxis.

stem: A 69-year-old man complains of shortness of breath and weight loss for the last 6 months. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and no TB or HIV risk factors (see reports). Chest X-ray: A large left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: 1,500 mL of bloody fluid that is strongly exudative by Light's criteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 69-year-old, 40 pack-year smoker with 6 months of weight loss and a large bloody exudative effusion most likely has lung cancer (or pleural malignancy). The next step is contrast CT of the chest to show the underlying mass, nodes and pleural thickening and to plan an image-guided biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Empirical antibiotics suit a parapneumonic effusion with fever, cough and raised inflammatory markers, not a bloody effusion with months of weight loss.
C. Blind pleural biopsy has low yield; when malignancy is suspected, biopsy should be CT-guided or thoracoscopic after CT has mapped the pleura.
key_concept:
Pleural effusion work-up:
  • Step 1: diagnostic thoracentesis, apply Light's criteria
  • Transudate: treat the cause (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic)
  • Exudate unexplained: contrast CT chest
  • Suspected malignancy: CT-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy
  • Bloody effusion: malignancy, trauma, PE, TB
exam_pearl: Smoker + weight loss + bloody exudate = malignancy until proven otherwise; image before you biopsy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0674).

stem: A 69-year-old man complains of shortness of breath and weight loss for the last 6 months. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and no TB or HIV risk factors (see reports). Chest X-ray: A large left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: 1,500 mL of bloody fluid that is strongly exudative by Light's criteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 69 year old, 40 pack year smoker with 6 months of weight loss and a large bloody, strongly exudative effusion has malignancy (lung cancer or mesothelioma) until proven otherwise. After the tap has been done, contrast CT chest is the next step: it shows the underlying mass, pleural thickening or nodules and lymph nodes, and maps the best target for a guided biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Empirical antibiotics fit a parapneumonic effusion or empyema (fever, acute illness, purulent or low pH fluid). Six months of weight loss with a bloody effusion is not an infection picture.
C. Tissue is eventually needed, but a pleural biopsy should be image guided (CT guided or thoracoscopic) and planned after the CT; a blind biopsy before imaging has a lower yield.
key_concept:
Exudative effusion work up order:
  • Diagnostic thoracentesis: Light's criteria, cytology, culture, cell count
  • Suspected malignancy → contrast CT chest (ideally before draining the fluid fully)
  • Then tissue: CT guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy, or biopsy of the primary
  • Bloody effusion: malignancy, PE, trauma, TB
exam_pearl: Smoker + weight loss + bloody exudate → CT chest with contrast before any biopsy.
